meaning: A policy built on a model that already reads images and text. It also takes an instruction in words and the robot's joint readings as input, and it outputs an action chunk.
A network pretrained on images and text from the web. It takes pictures and a prompt as input and writes text.
The vision-language model inside a VLA. It turns the camera images and the instruction into tokens and reads them once per call.
The smaller network in a VLA that outputs the action chunk. It reads the backbone's results through attention, together with the robot's state. Physical Intelligence calls it the action expert.
Physical Intelligence's name for the action head.
The sentence that tells a VLA which task to do. The model receives it on every call.
The sequence of image tokens and text tokens that enters the backbone on one call. The backbone reads it once, and its results are cached for the action head.
Filling the unused slots of a fixed-width state or action vector with zeros, so that one model can serve robots with different numbers of joints.
A robot body, with its joints, sensors and action space.
A way to generate an action chunk: the model starts from random noise and refines it in a few steps. Section 4, Learning From Demonstrations, covers it.
One refinement pass of the action head on its way from noise to an action chunk. It is also called a refinement step.
A transformer used to refine noise into an output, which in a VLA is an action chunk.
NVIDIA's name for the slow side of a robot model: the vision-language model that reads the scene and the instruction.
NVIDIA's name for the fast side of a robot model: the action head, which turns the slow side's output and the robot's state into actions.
Times per second.
A model that predicts future video and the action chunk together. It forecasts what the camera will see as well as what the robot should do.
A fine-tune that adds small matrices to the model and trains only those, leaving the original weights frozen.
A small policy trained from scratch on demonstrations of one task. Section 4, Learning From Demonstrations, covers it.
Video shot from the point of view of the person doing the task.
A suite of simulated manipulation tasks used as a benchmark for robot policies.
NVIDIA's compiler that turns a trained network into an optimised inference engine.
Physical Intelligence's open repository. It holds pi0, pi0-FAST and pi0.5.
Hugging Face's open robotics library. It trains and runs policies on arms such as the SO-101.
One model family in LeRobot, which you select on the command line with --policy.type.
An NVIDIA onboard computer for robots. The GR00T N1.7 model card calls it Jetson AGX Thor.
One vector that a transformer processes. An image patch or a piece of a word becomes one token.
One of the small squares that a camera image is cut into. Each patch becomes one token.
The transformer operation in which one token reads information from other tokens. The action head uses it to read the backbone's results.
The run of future actions that a policy returns in one call. Section 4, Learning From Demonstrations, covers it.
In the figure of the two clocks, one backbone pass over the scene and the instruction.
A set of learned vectors that is fed to the model for one robot type. X-VLA uses soft prompts to serve many robot bodies.
Describes weights that a fine-tune does not update. Frozen weights need no gradient and no optimiser state in GPU memory.
Describes a model whose numbers are stored at lower precision, which makes it smaller and faster.
The name NVIDIA gives to the number format of its quantised GR00T N1.7 build.
Two kinds of test. In distribution, the object starts in positions that the demonstrations covered. Out of distribution, it starts somewhere new.
The computer that the arm and its cameras plug into. It plays one action from the chunk per tick.
A public set of labelled photos. ACT's ResNet-18 image backbone starts from weights trained on it.
